passage: On Monday at the park in Uppsala, Ulla watched Fatima walk up to three children building a sand castle. "Can I play too?" Fatima asked, and they moved over to make room. Ulla stayed on the bench, holding her spade. On Tuesday the same children were at the sandpit. Ulla walked over, smiled, and said the exact words: "Can I play too?" A boy handed her a bucket.

qa.q: What did the boy hand Ulla?
qa.a: A bucket.

qa.q: What was Ulla feeling on Monday, holding her spade on the bench?
qa.a: She was probably shy and unsure, wanting to join but not knowing how.

qa.q: What else could Ulla try if the words didn't work?
qa.a: She could offer something, like her spade, or start digging nearby and wait to be asked.

qa.q: How might Fatima feel if she saw Ulla use her words?
qa.a: Fatima might feel pleased and proud that her way helped someone else.

grounding: A child watches another join a group by asking "Can I play too?" and uses the same words the next day at the sandpit, with a smile.

passage: At the school playground in Guwahati, Ramesh saw Irawati walk up to the skipping group and ask, "Can I play too?" They made space. The next day at recess, Ramesh went to the sandpit where four children were digging. He smiled, took a breath, and said, "Can I play too?" One girl moved her bucket. "Sure. Dig here."

qa.q: Where did Ramesh go the next day?
qa.a: He went to the sandpit.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when he took a breath?
qa.a: He was probably nervous but hopeful, using the words that worked for Irawati.

qa.q: What else could Ramesh do to join another time?
qa.a: He could bring something to share or offer to help, not only ask.

qa.q: How does Ramesh's question look to the girl who moved her bucket?
qa.a: It is easy for her to say yes, since he asked politely with a smile.

grounding: A child copies a classmate's way of joining, asking "Can I play too?" the next day at the sandpit with a smile.

passage: Ada's new bicycle was red, with a bell. In the courtyard of the Lagos flats, Fatima stared at it. "Want to play tag?" Ada asked. Fatima shook her head, still staring at the bike. Ada thought. "You can have the first ride. Then we play tag." Fatima's eyes lit up. "Deal!" She rode to the gate and back, rang the bell twice and hopped off. "You're it!"

qa.q: What colour was Ada's bicycle?
qa.a: It was red, with a bell.

qa.q: What was Ada thinking when she offered the first ride?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and clever, guessing Fatima wanted the bike more than tag.

qa.q: What else could Ada offer if Fatima still said no?
qa.a: She could ask what Fatima wants to play, since trading works best when she knows what her friend wants.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Fatima?
qa.a: Fatima is thrilled because she gets the bike first, so tag feels worth it.

grounding: A child offers a friend the first ride on her new bicycle in return for playing tag afterwards.

passage: In the community centre hall, Ritu had the new tricycle that everyone wanted. Tarun hovered near the door. "Play tag with me?" Ritu asked. Tarun shrugged and looked at the trike. Ritu climbed off. "You go first on the trike, two rounds. Then tag." Tarun grinned and pedalled round the hall twice. Then he jumped off and tagged her. "You're it!"

qa.q: How many rounds did Tarun pedal?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Ritu thinking when she climbed off?
qa.a: She felt hopeful that giving Tarun the trike first would get him to play tag.

qa.q: What else could Ritu try with a friend who wants something different?
qa.a: Ask what the friend wants and then trade, as she did with the trike.

qa.q: How does Ritu's offer feel to Tarun?
qa.a: Tarun is happy and eager, since he gets the trike first.

grounding: A child offers a friend the first turn on a tricycle in exchange for playing tag afterwards.

passage:
Monday: Damini wanted to play hopscotch with Sunita, but when Sunita said no, Damini went home crying.
Wednesday: on the way out she thought, If Sunita says no, I'll ask Vaibhav. Sunita said no. Damini went straight to Vaibhav.
Friday: before going down, she told Mummy, "Sunita first, then Vaibhav, then anyone."

qa.q: Who did Damini go to on Wednesday?
qa.a: She went straight to Vaibhav.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling on Monday when Sunita said no?
qa.a: She was upset and sad, and went home crying.

qa.q: What else could Damini add to her plan?
qa.a: She could have a game she can play alone, just in case everyone is busy.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel being asked second?
qa.a: He would probably be happy to be asked and may not mind being second.

grounding: Over several days a child learns to plan a second choice before asking a friend to play, so a refusal doesn't end the plan.

passage: The park would close in fifteen minutes, and Dilnaz wanted a game. She looked at Arohi, who was on the swings. If she says no, I'll ask the twins by the slide, Dilnaz thought. "Arohi, want to play catch?" "Not now." Dilnaz didn't wait. She ran to the slide. "Want to play catch?" The twins nodded. They played till the whistle blew.

qa.q: How long until the park closed?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz thinking before she asked Arohi?
qa.a: She felt ready and hopeful, with a backup plan in case Arohi said no.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz try if the twins also said no?
qa.a: She could ask to join what they are already playing, since that might be easier.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel seeing Dilnaz play with the twins?
qa.a: Arohi might feel fine, since she wanted to swing, or a little left out.

grounding: A child prepares a second choice before asking a friend to play, so a refusal doesn't end her plan.

passage: I'm Naveen, Arohi's cousin, and I was reading on the bed. Arohi sat on the floor holding her doll. "Do you want to play?" she whispered to it. Then again, a little louder: "Do you want to play?" She put the doll down and walked out to the colony lane. Through the window I watched her go up to a girl with a ball and say it. I don't know how nervous she was, but her hands were fists.

qa.q: What was Naveen doing?
qa.a: Naveen was reading on the bed.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as he watched Arohi through the window?
qa.a: Naveen was curious and a little anxious for Arohi, noticing her hands were fists.

qa.q: What else could help Arohi if she feels shy?
qa.a: Practising a second line too, like "Can I have a turn?", so she has more to say.

qa.q: What might saying the words for real be like for Arohi?
qa.a: It is probably scary but easier after practising with the doll.

grounding: An observer watches a shy child practise asking "Do you want to play?" with a doll before going out and saying it to a real child.

passage:
Monday: Nitin watched the boys in the lane but stayed at the gate, silent.
Tuesday: in his room he held up his teddy. "Do you want to play?" he said. He said it three times, each time louder.
Thursday: he walked to the lane, found Pranav bouncing a ball and said, "Do you want to play?" Pranav tossed him the ball.

qa.q: What did Nitin hold up on Tuesday?
qa.a: He held up his teddy.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling on Monday at the gate?
qa.a: He was shy and nervous about joining the boys.

qa.q: What else could Nitin try if Pranav said no?
qa.a: He could ask another boy, or practise another line like "Can I join?"

qa.q: How does Nitin's question look to Pranav?
qa.a: Pranav finds it a simple, friendly question and answers by tossing the ball.

grounding: Over several days a shy child practises asking "Do you want to play?" with a teddy, then says it to a real child.

passage: At the kindergarten playground, Tenzin went to Rehana ma'am. "Nobody wants to play with me." His voice was very small. Rehana ma'am knelt. "Hmm. Let's start a game that everyone can play." She clapped her hands. "Who wants to play duck, duck, goose?" Children ran over. She sat Tenzin in the circle. He was first to be picked as goose.

qa.q: What game did Rehana ma'am start?
qa.a: Duck, duck, goose.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he told Rehana ma'am?
qa.a: He was lonely and sad, speaking in a very small voice.

qa.q: What else could help Tenzin join by himself next time?
qa.a: Learning a line like "Can I play too?", so he has a way in when no teacher is near.

qa.q: How does the moment look to Rehana ma'am?
qa.a: Rehana ma'am sees a child who needs help getting in, so she makes a game that includes him.

grounding: A child tells the teacher nobody wants to play, and the teacher starts a group game that gives him a way in.

passage: I'm Ojas, and I'm in Kavitha's class. At recess she stood by the wall alone. Then she went to our teacher and said something. I heard "nobody" and "play". The teacher called out, "Everyone, let's play statue!" and held Kavitha's hand. We all played. Kavitha laughed when she froze in a funny pose. I think she was sad before, but I'm not sure.

qa.q: What game did the teacher call out?
qa.a: Statue.

qa.q: What was Ojas thinking about Kavitha?
qa.a: Ojas felt unsure but guessed she was sad before, and noticed she laughed later.

qa.q: What else could Ojas do to help Kavitha?
qa.a: Ojas could ask Kavitha to play next recess, so she doesn't need a teacher.

qa.q: What might the statue game have meant for Kavitha?
qa.a: It gave her a way in, which likely made her feel included and happy.

grounding: An observer describes a child who tells the teacher nobody will play with her, and the teacher starts a group game.

passage: Under the peepal tree in the village school yard, Pallavi stood with her hands on her hips. "Varun, you have to play house. Or I'm not your friend." Varun looked at her, then at the boys playing marbles. He said nothing, turned, and walked to the marbles. Pallavi stamped her foot. "Fine!" But nobody came to play house.

qa.q: What were the boys playing?
qa.a: Marbles.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: She was angry and hurt that Varun walked away.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Pallavi asked?
qa.a: Offer instead of demand, like "Want to play house? You can be the father," since threats push friends away.

qa.q: How does Pallavi's demand feel to Varun?
qa.a: It feels bossy and unfair, so he chooses the marbles.

grounding: A child tells her friend he must play her game or she won't be his friend, and he walks away.

passage: On the pavement outside their building in Lisbon, Rafael blocked Rania's way. "You have to play pirates, or I won't be your friend." Rania stared at him. Then she walked off to the chalk drawings with the others. Rafael shouted, "Fine, then!" and kicked a pebble. He played pirates alone until dinner.

qa.q: What did Rania walk off to?
qa.a: The chalk drawings with the others.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when he kicked the pebble?
qa.a: He was angry and lonely after Rania walked away.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Rafael better?
qa.a: Inviting Rania nicely or joining the chalk drawings, because demands push friends away.

qa.q: How does the demand look to Rania?
qa.a: It feels bossy and unkind, so she chooses to leave.

grounding: A child demands that his friend play his game or lose his friendship, and she walks away.

subtype: Approach: giving up after one no [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Hrithik, and Madhav lives next door. Yesterday he knocked on Sachin's door and asked him to play. Sachin said, "Not now, I'm eating." Madhav walked back slowly and sat on the stairs with his chin on his knees. I asked what happened. "Nobody likes me," he said. I don't know if he really believes it, but he stayed on the stairs a long time.

qa.q: What was Sachin doing when Madhav asked?
qa.a: He was eating.

qa.q: What was Hrithik thinking as Madhav sat on the stairs?
qa.a: Hrithik felt worried and unsure whether Madhav really believed nobody liked him.

qa.q: What else could Madhav try after a "not now"?
qa.a: He could ask again later, or ask Hrithik, since "not now" isn't "never".

qa.q: What might "not now" have meant to Madhav?
qa.a: To Madhav it felt like a big rejection, so he was hurt and sad.

grounding: An observer describes a child who hears "not now" from a friend, decides nobody likes him, and sits alone.

subtype: Approach: giving up after one no [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday: Shankar asked Nandini to play ball. "Not now," she said, busy with her drawing. Shankar sat alone by the door. "Nobody likes me," he told Amma.
Saturday: Amma said, "Not now means later." Shankar asked Nandini again after lunch. She said yes.
Monday: Nandini said, "Not now." Shankar said, "Okay, later?" and went to swing.

qa.q: What was Nandini busy with on Friday?
qa.a: Her drawing.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling on Friday by the door?
qa.a: He was sad and lonely, believing nobody liked him.

qa.q: What helped Shankar change, and why?
qa.a: Amma explaining that "not now" means later, which helped him ask again instead of giving up.

qa.q: How does Shankar's change look to Nandini?
qa.a: Nandini gets to finish her drawing and still play with him later.

grounding: Over several days a child learns that one "not now" is not the final word and stops reading it as rejection.

passage: At the school playground, Rashmi joined the queue for the slide. She counted the heads in front of her: "One, two, three." "Three more, then me," she said to Lavanya, behind her. When one child slid down, she said, "Two more." Then "One more." She bounced on her toes. "Me!" and she whooshed down.

qa.q: How many children were in front of Rashmi at first?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling as she bounced on her toes?
qa.a: She was excited and impatient, knowing her turn was next.

qa.q: What else could Rashmi do to make waiting easier?
qa.a: Chat with Lavanya or play a quick game while counting, so the time passes faster.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see Rashmi's counting?
qa.a: Lavanya may find it helpful and start counting too.

grounding: A child counts the children ahead at the slide and works out her place, which makes waiting easier.

passage: I'm Chetan, and my cousin Vaibhav came to the park with me. At the slide there was a long line. Vaibhav counted the children in front. "Three more," he said. After one went down he said, "Two." He didn't push or whine; he just kept counting, fingers up. When he said "Me!" he sounded so happy. I think counting helped him wait.

qa.q: How many children were in front of Vaibhav at first?
qa.a: Three more.

qa.q: What was Chetan thinking about the counting?
qa.a: Chetan felt impressed and thought the counting helped Vaibhav wait.

qa.q: What else could help Vaibhav wait in a longer line?
qa.a: He could chat or play a small game while counting, so the wait feels shorter.

qa.q: How did it feel for Vaibhav when it was his turn?
qa.a: He was very happy and excited, saying "Me!"

grounding: An observer describes a child who counts the children ahead at the slide, which helps him wait calmly.

passage: The swing in the colony park had a line. Nilesh waited behind Aryan. Then a bigger boy ran up and jumped on the swing ahead of everyone. Nilesh's face went red. He marched to Manjula ma'am, the park helper. "He didn't wait his turn!" Manjula ma'am looked, nodded and walked over. "The line is here. Back of the line, please." The big boy slid off.

qa.q: Who did Nilesh go to?
qa.a: Manjula ma'am, the park helper.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when his face went red?
qa.a: He was angry and felt it was unfair that the boy skipped the line.

qa.q: What else could Nilesh try if no adult were there?
qa.a: He could say clearly to the boy, "We're waiting in a line," before going to an adult.

qa.q: How does the skip look to Manjula ma'am?
qa.a: She sees it as unfair and fixes it quickly, sending the boy to the back.

grounding: A child asks an adult to settle whose turn it is after another child skips ahead on the swing.

passage:
"Ma'am! Ma'am!" Noor ran to the teacher.
"What is it?"
"Irfan didn't wait his turn! He jumped on the swing!"
"Was he in the line?"
"No! We were all waiting."
"Let's go and see."
At the swing, the teacher said, "Irfan, the line starts behind Noor."
Irfan got off and grumbled, "Okay."

qa.q: What did Irfan do?
qa.a: He jumped on the swing without waiting his turn.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she ran to the teacher?
qa.a: She was upset and felt it was unfair that Irfan skipped the line.

qa.q: What else could Noor try before telling the teacher?
qa.a: She could tell Irfan herself, "The line is here," and ask the teacher only if he won't listen.

qa.q: How does the moment look to Irfan?
qa.a: Irfan is probably embarrassed and a bit annoyed at being sent to the back.

grounding: A child asks the teacher to settle whose turn it is when another child skips ahead on the swing.

passage: The park had only one swing, and it was getting dark. Sahil and his brother Lalit both wanted it. "Twenty pushes, then off," Lalit said. "Okay," said Sahil. He climbed on. Lalit pushed and Sahil counted out loud: "One, two, three..." At "twenty" he dragged his feet and hopped off. "Your turn!" They both had a go before the gate closed.

qa.q: How many pushes did they agree on?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he hopped off?
qa.a: He seemed happy and fair, ready to give Lalit his turn.

qa.q: What else could the boys agree if there was less time?
qa.a: Ten pushes each, so both still get a go before the gate closes.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Lalit?
qa.a: Lalit finds it fair and clear, so there is no fight.

grounding: Two brothers agree in advance that one gets off after twenty pushes, and the counted rule prevents a fight.

passage: On the swing in the Bengaluru colony park, Tanvir begged, "Just a bit longer!" Tarun, his friend, frowned. "You always say that." Tanvir thought. "If I get twenty pushes, then I get off. Deal?" "Deal." Tarun pushed. Tanvir counted aloud, "...eighteen, nineteen, twenty!" He slid off. "Your turn, Tarun!"

qa.q: What did Tanvir count up to?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he slid off?
qa.a: He was cheerful and satisfied, having had his twenty pushes.

qa.q: What else could help if Tanvir forgets the deal?
qa.a: Tarun could count aloud too, so both keep track of the rule.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Tarun?
qa.a: Tarun is relieved because he knows when his turn will come.

grounding: A child agrees to get off the swing after twenty pushes and counts aloud, so getting off is less of a fight.
